courses.description: English 9 is designed to expand a student’s understanding of literature, including both classics and modern selections in the various genres. This course also stresses the continued improvement of writing skills with special emphasis on organization and development.

This course is a continuation of the skills developed in English 9. Writing skills will continue to be a focus, as well as vocabulary and literature. Literature will be genre based with connections to world and classical literature explored. This course includes extensive literature study, and students will be expected to do reading outside of class.

English 11 will focus on American Literature with emphasis on critical analysis, which focuses on the standards and grade level expectations, with writing assignments designed for the students to continue their development as discriminating learners. There will be an emphasis placed on research of both primary and secondary documents. This course will prepare students to successfully complete college-type research, analysis, and writing.

English 12 explores primarily British literary types and themes. The course continues with the basic principles of critical writing. Included are literature based essays and analytical investigations designed to improve students’ literary perception and writing styles. College level work is developed.

Public Speaking is designed to provide students with an abundance of opportunities to speak, in a variety of forms, in front of audiences of people. Students will read and study both vocal and body techniques that contribute to effective presentations. Reading, research, note taking and speech writing are emphasized; as well, students will explore dramatic kinds of speaking such as monologues, dialogues and other theatrical performance. The focus of the course is to provide students with opportunities to speak often and in return receive both peer and teacher feedback in an effort to help develop poised communicators.

For the purposes of this class, we need to make film viewing an active enterprise. We will watch a wealth of films from a variety of genres and directed from a variety of points-of-view. This course will give you exposure to ideas and ways of expressing those ideas in film that you may never choose/have chosen on your own. Course objectives/learning outcomes: developing skills in observation, analysis, interpretation, evaluation, expression, writing and critical thinking.

Civics will examine what it means to be an American. Students will learn about the foundations of the American political system, and what values and principles are basic to American constitutional democracy. Students will learn about the relationship we as citizens have with our government and will examine the rights and responsibilities of citizens. The course also examines the structure of the U.S. government and how it functions.

Global Studies will examine world history, world cultures, and international relations from the 1400s into modern times. Emphasis will be placed on current events as they relate to historical events. This course is designed to give students opportunities to learn about our increasingly interdependent world.

U.S. History is a survey of US history from the Civil War era to modern times. Topics may include industrialization, immigration, globalization, war and peace, and significant political, socioeconomic, and cultural developments in the U.S. since the Civil War.

Modern U.S. History will examine U.S. history since 1945. This class will discuss post World War II American society and culture, the Cold War, expanding U.S. foreign relations, Korean War, Vietnam, the social/political movements of the 1960s, America’s involvement in the Middle East, the divide between liberalism and conservatism, and the evolution of modern American culture.

Comparative religion is an introduction to the comparative study of major religious traditions from primal to modern. Included is an overview of classical religions, such as Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism, Islam, Judaism, and Christianity. Attention is also given to social forces affecting religion and religion’s impact on history, individuals and society.

The purpose of this course is to satisfy Algebra 1A requirements of the Common Core Mathematics Standards adopted by the State of Vermont. This course fits into an overall program of mathematics studies with a rigorous academic core by extending what students have learned in the prior level mathematics courses as well as introducing more advanced topics. The Mathematical Practice Standards apply throughout each the course and together with the content standards, prescribe that students experience mathematics as a coherent, useful and logical subject that makes use of their ability to make sense of problem situation.

In this course students will review if necessary linear relations, including some work with best-fit lines. Students will then explore non-linear relations such as exponential growth, exponential decay and quadratics. Other topics include polynomials, solving linear systems by different methods, and an introduction to functions covering the topics of notation, domain and range.

This course integrates coordinates and transformations throughout and gives strong attention to measurement formulas and three-dimensional figures in the first part of the course. Work with proof-writing follows a carefully sequenced development of the logical and conceptual precursors to proof. Technology is used throughout the course.

This course emphasizes facility with algebraic expressions and forms, especially linear and quadratic forms, powers and roots and functions based on these concepts. Students study logarithmic, polynomial, and other special functions both for their abstract properties and as tools for modeling real-world situations. Technology for graphing functions will be available to students.

Pre-Calculus through Mathematical Modeling. The course is organized into six major units of study that develop understanding of the nature of functions, their properties, and their applications. Students will investigate modeling with linear, exponential, logarithmic, power, polynomial, rational and trigonometric functions. Matrix mathematics will be explored and the course will finish with probability, sequences, applications of Fibonacci numbers in a wide variety of settings, and other recursively based topics.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra 2 and recommendation of teacher.

courses.description: An introduction to the basic ideas and techniques of probability and statistics. Topics may include numerical and graphical descriptive measures, probability, random variables, the normal distribution, sampling theory, estimation, hypothesis testing, correlation and regression. The use of technology may be required. Students must take a math assessment for placement purposes prior to registration.

The foundations level course is for students who need to develop basic and functional life skills in math. These are students who will benefit from small group or individual lessons and a hands-on approach to learning. This course is designed for those students requiring instruction in basic knowledge of math for everyday living, as well as those needing to master basic skills. Units will vary yearly depending on the needs of the students in the class. Examples of units include, financial math: banking, employment, budgeting, consumer skills, credit and debit, financing; basic operations related to life skills or specific career paths; other topics related to specific needs of individual students. This course may be taken for multiple years for credit, with different topics each semester.

Algebra, Geometry, and Statistics. This course requires students to participate in investigations leading to: the understanding of data collection, data representation, and data interpretation; the introduction and use of linear, exponential, equations; the understanding of three-dimensional geometry through the study of surface area and volume; tessellations and nets of solids; volume and linear models of data; exponential growth; areas, volumes direct and inverse proportions. The course will also review the basic skills of arithmetic, number properties, and basic geometric concepts of two-dimensional geometry. Students will further their understanding of mathematical concepts through investigations and discussions that apply and use mathematics.

Algebra, Geometry and Statistics. This course requires students to participate in investigations leading to: inequalities and linear programming, matrix operations, Pythagorean Theorem and right triangle trigonometry, probability, volume and surface areas. the study of geometry through right triangle trigonometry, volume and surface area, and transformational geometry; the retaining emphasis on the presentation and interpretation of data, through the study of measures of central tendency, apportionment, and sampling; and the introduction of exponential laws and models, function transformations, limits of sequences and matrices. The course will also review the basics skill of arithmetic, number properties, and basic geometric concepts of two-dimensional geometry. Students will further their understanding of mathematical concepts through investigations and discussions that apply and use mathematics.

Algebra, Geometry and Statistics. This course requires students to participate in investigations leading to: probability; volume and surface area; linear programming and solving systems of equations; negative and fractional exponents; geometric properties; the study of trigonometric ratios and functions; polynomial functions; inequalities and pre-limit notions; rational functions; function transformations; conic sections; and combinatories. The course will also review basic skills of arithmetic, number properties and basic geometric concepts of two-dimensional geometry. Students will further their understanding of mathematical concepts through investigations and discussions that apply and use mathematics.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Math 1 and 2

courses.description: Algebra, Geometry and Statistics This course requires students to participate in investigations leading to: three dimensional coordinate systems; trigonometric ratios in general triangles; combinatories; linear and quadratic functions; modeling data; and mathematics of finance. The course will also review basic skills of arithmetic, number properties, and basic geometric concepts of two-dimensional geometry. Students will further their understanding of mathematical concepts through investigations and discussions that apply and use mathematics.

Earth Science is the study of the world around you. Our topics will include astronomy (study of outer space), geology (study of rocks, earthquakes, volcanoes, plate tectonics, and history of the Earth), meteorology (study of the atmosphere, climate, and climate change), and human sustainability (natural hazards, natural resources, and environmental impact of human activities). We look closely at the Big Bang Theory, how we mine for materials in a sustainable manner, climate change, and a lab project focused around weathering of Earth’s surface. Recommended for 9th grade.

Biology is the scientific study of living organisms. Students participating in this course will develop an understanding of the principles of biology including, lab safety, scientific processes, ecology, cells, genetics, evolution and the six kingdoms. The course considers the interactions among the vast number of organisms that inhabit planet Earth. It presents the basic form and function of these organisms, from cells to organ systems, and simple to complex cellular structure. It delves into interactions between organisms, and between an organism and its environment. Laboratory work, hands-on activities and some dissections will help students on their journey through the amazing living world. Recommended for 10th grade.

Chemistry is the study of the composition and properties of substances, and the changes that such substances can undergo. Students will explore the fundamental principles of chemistry which characterize the properties of matter and how it reacts. Like all sciences, the science of chemistry is an organized and systematic attempt to understand the world around us. Chemists make careful observations about the world, generating questions which they seek to answer. Then they test possible answers, or hypotheses, through experimentation. We will use this basic strategy to examine the main categories in chemistry. Through many activities students will demonstrate how theory is applicable in laboratory situations. All students will develop good methods of problem solving and proper laboratory technique. Topics include, but are not limited to: measurement, atomic structure, electron configuration, the periodic table bonding, gas laws, properties of liquids and solids, solutions, stoichiometry, reactions, kinetics, equilibrium, and acids and bases. Recommended for 11th grade.

This course is designed to introduce the student to practical applications of chemistry, physics, and biology in the study of forensics. This course will provide students with an introduction to the human body as well as a theoretical understanding and practical application of forensic science techniques. Topics covered in this course include forensic DNA typing, bloodstain pattern analysis, forensic entomology, forensic toxicology, drugs and poisons, forensic anthropology, crime scene investigations, evidence collection and examination, and career opportunities in forensics. Strong emphasis is placed on in-person lab participation. Recommended for 11th and 12th grade.

These half credit courses will focus on basic physics concepts including forces and interactions, energy, and waves, electricity, and electromagnetism along with crosscutting concepts from various science courses. Concepts will be related to the world around us through discussion, labs, and projects. This course will rely heavily on project based learning, such as an egg drop, bridge building, clean energy design, rollercoaster, and mouse trap cars. Strong emphasis is placed on in-person lab participation. Recommended for 10th grade and up. (alternating odd years)

The Marine Biology course builds upon and extends biological concepts developed during earlier science courses. Students take an in depth look at the physical, chemical, and geological characteristics of the world’s oceans. They then investigate the structure, functions, behaviors, adaptations, and classification of a variety of plants and animals that live in the marine environment. Students learn how energy flows and matter cycles through the Earth’s ocean system and they investigate the impact of humans on that system. Laboratory activities include dissection, experimentation, data collection, and data analysis that develop scientific investigation and scientific thinking skills.

courses.description: These half credit courses will investigate the history of science fiction films as well as the real science that inspires these great cinematic adventures. From technology and transportation to time travel and titan animals we will explore the world of science fiction from page to film. This course is focused on project based learning through the lens of science topics in life and physical science. Students can take section I, section II, or both for credit. Strong emphasis is placed on in-person lab participation.

courses.description: This course will focus heavily on human activity and the impact on Earth weather and climate. Data sets, weather patterns, and climate will be analyzed in order to draw conclusions and make predictions. Projects will include quantitative modeling of the carbon cycle, weather prediction, hazardous weather research, and evaluation of alternative energy options. Successful completion of Earth Science required. Strong emphasis is placed on in-person lab participation. (alternating even years)
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Earth Science required.

courses.description: Astronomy is the scientific study of the contents of the Universe. This course will focus on the history of astronomy, how we observe the universe, formation and motion of the solar system and stars, and space exploration. Projects will include designing a telescope, rocket launching, and a space shelter challenge. Strong emphasis is placed on in-person lab participation. Successful completion of Earth Science required. (alternating even years)

courses.description: Students will learn to understand spoken French using vocabulary and constructions appropriate for the earliest phases of language learning. Students will be able to answer questions, and ask these questions in the appropriate situations. Students will follow and carry on basic conversations using familiar construction and vocabulary. Students will read and write all material learned orally. Countries in which French is spoken will be explored.

Students will review and expand upon vocabulary and constructions previously studied. French will be used increasingly in class. Reading and writing skills will be developed. Works in French will be read. Cultural elements will be introduced and current events will be explored on an on-going basis.

Students will learn to understand spoken Spanish using vocabulary and constructions appropriate for the earliest phases of language learning. Students will be able to answer questions, and ask these questions in the appropriate situations. Students will follow and carry on basic conversations using familiar construction and vocabulary. Students will read and write all material learned orally. Countries in which Spanish is spoken will be explored.

Students will review and expand upon vocabulary and constructions previously studied. Spanish will be used increasingly in class. Reading and writing skills will be developed. Works in Spanish will be read. Cultural elements will be introduced in Spanish. Current events will be explored on an on-going basis.

Students will continue to review and develop vocabulary and learn more complex structures and concepts inherent to Spanish. Students will speak Spanish in class. Journal writing and individual language projects will be emphasized. Literature will continue to be explored and additional works read.

courses.description: The mission of this class is to prepare individuals to be competent, confident and caring in managing their personal, family and career lives. The course content includes: body structure, human growth and development, family and mental health, nutrition, prevention of disease, safety, a personal health habits, drugs and alcohol. The skills that will be developed in this class are: decision making, communication skills, examination of values and attitudes, location and evaluation of health related information, application and coping skills.
courses.fulfills_text: 2 physical education credits and 1 health credit are required for graduation.

courses.description: Students in physical education classes follow a structured curriculum focusing on two areas: individual/team sports and introduction to fitness. The individual/team sports curriculum includes a variety of activities designed to enhance self-confidence, group dynamics, and coordination and movement skills. The introduction to fitness curriculum focuses on the five components of fitness, instructing students in the basics of exercise physiology and providing insight into the importance of leading an active lifestyle. Students are assessed on their ability to successfully complete required activities and class projects. Teachers use a grading rubric to help students understand expectations and track performance. As in all physical education classes, each student will be evaluated on participation, attitude, projects and/or written test.
courses.fulfills_text: 2 physical education credits and 1 health credit are required for graduation.

courses.description: Personal fitness is based completely on each individual student's goals. It covers numerous topics throughout the semester, focusing on the Five Components of Fitness. Once individual goals are created the student will research the best types of exercises to perform. Nutrition will also be discussed. The overall goal for this course is to teach students to create their own workout plans, eat healthier, and be prepared to continue exercising on their own after the course and after they graduate high school.
courses.fulfills_text: 2 physical education credits and 1 health credit are required for graduation.

courses.description: This course will cover the basics of art with a developing understanding of the elements and principles of design. Students will learn a variety of 2-dimensional techniques using pencils, pastels, watercolor, acrylics, printmaking, and collage. They will also discover 3-dimensional techniques through papier mache, clay, paper, and wood. Homework will be due weekly and will cover artists and/or cultures related to the project being created. In addition students will learn how to build their own professional art portfolio and utilize Google tools. This course is a pre-requisite to all 820 or higher level art classes.

courses.description: This class will take pencils and paint to a whole new level. Students will develop advanced techniques with pencils, pastels, watercolor, acrylics, and oils. They will create realistic, abstract, and non-representational work. Would you like to have more than one piece of your art to share? Do you yearn to try new and unusual materials? Students will develop advanced techniques in printmaking through linoleum and wood block, as well as etchings, and monotypes. Homework will be due weekly and will cover artists and/or cultures related to the project being created. In addition students will learn how to build their own professional art portfolio, take part in class critiques, and utilize Google tools. Students will spend the last part of the semester in independent studio to gain proficiency in a chosen media. (alternating years)

Students will observe how pottery has been used by a variety of cultures and understand how it has evolved over time. In addition students will learn how to build their own professional art portfolio and utilize Google tools.

courses.description: This course is a performance-based class where the basic skills of instrument playing are taught and refined. Listening, improvising, and self and group reflection are included in the curriculum. Once a week, students are required to attend a small-group/individual lesson where group/individualized instruction is given to work on band music. Extra lessons will be available for students who choose to participate in festivals, other performance audition groups or who want to challenge themselves beyond the band music. Students progress at their own speed according to their experience level upon entering the class. Beginners as well as more advanced students are welcome. The Poultney High School Band performs at area parades, winter and spring concerts, and other performance field trips which all band students are all required to attend.

Extra lessons will be available for students who choose to participate in festivals or other performance audition groups. Chorus performances include the Poultney High School Winter and Spring Concerts and performance field trips which all chorus students are required to attend. No prior musical experience is necessary to be in chorus, and everyone is welcome.

Classroom topics include the study of musical notation and symbols, the performance of simple melodies, standard scales and chord progressions, folk songs, and popular music. Students will have public and class performances throughout the semester. Performances include classroom performances, a midterm performance and a final recital performance.

courses.description: Driver Education is not a graduation requirement but is mandated by the State of Vermont before you can obtain your Vermont driver’s license. The program is offered free through the school, or may be taken for a fee outside of school with private contractors. Students must be 15 and have a valid learner’s permit. Students must complete a minimum of 30 hours of classroom, instruction, with 6 hours of in-car, and 18 hours of observation. The acquisition of appropriate knowledge, proper habits and skill development will assist in developing sound personal attitudes. courses.description: Students may only take an online course if the course is not offered at PoHS or 2) there is a course conflict within their schedule. If the course is offered at PoHS and there is no schedule conflict, students must take the course with a PoHS teacher. Students who take VHS online courses must be prepared to communicate regularly with their instructor. Participation in online courses requires students to be self-disciplined and responsible enough to work independently. It is the student’s responsibility to log on, complete and submit all work, and communicate with the course instructor if applicable. PHS offers online courses through The VHS Collaborative & APEX programs. VHS is nationally accredited by the Middle States Commission on Secondary Education and the Northwest Accreditation Commission. Apex Learning Virtual School is accredited by the Northwest Accreditation Commission. Both programs offer classes for high school students from Advanced Placement courses to courses offered for remediation. Please contact the Guidance Director for more information.

With the Flexible Pathways bill (S.130/Act 77), dual enrollment vouchers allow Vermont high school students to take two college courses at any of 17 Vermont colleges or universities tuition-free. Students can use two vouchers throughout their junior and senior year but they must be used prior to graduation. Students will receive 1.0 HS credit per 3 credit college course upon the receipt of an official college transcript. Courses that are worth fewer than 3 college credits will receive 0.50 HS credits and courses worth 4 college credits will receive 1.5 HS credits.

courses.description: CCV offers a free, non-credit Introduction to College Studies (ICS) course for high school students each semester. ICS prepares you for college by helping you set goals, problem-solve, manage time and stress, improve communication skills, take better notes, reduce test anxiety, and plan financially. This course is recommended to be taken during the summer between a student’s sophomore and junior year. This course is in addition to the two free dual enrollment vouchers.

Vermont’s Early College Program allows high school seniors to take a full year of college-level classes while completing their high school degree. The Early College Program (ECP) simultaneously serves as a student's senior year of high school and first year of college. Students may take a year-long course of study in any discipline. This program is funded through the Flexible Pathways bill for approved colleges. Students who are accepted into an ECP must withdraw from Poultney High School prior to registering for enrollment at the college/university. Students will re-enroll at Poultney High School at the completion of their ECP in order to receive a Poultney High School diploma. Seniors will still be considered for Valedictorian and Salutatorian. Participating colleges/universities: Castleton University, Community College of Vermont, Goddard College, Northern Vermont University at Johnson or Lyndon, Norwich University and Vermont Technical College: Vermont Academy of Science and Technology.
